newsitem.title: USA: Jagermeister importer sued for harassment.
newsitem.headline: Jagermeister importer sued for harassment.

text.p: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Thursday sued the U.S. importer of Jagermeister liquor alleging the company's chairman and others sexually harassed more than 100 women, mostly models hired to promote the brand.
The suit, filed in Manhattan federal court, accuses Sidney Frank Importing Co. and Allstate Promotions Co., a company that markets the German-made Jagermeister, of sexual harassment and retaliation.

The EEOC is seeking unspecified damages for the women, including appropriate back pay with interest as well as compensation for pain, suffering and humiliation. It is also seeking punitive damages. The commission is also seeking a court order stopping the defendants from violating employment laws and forcing them to institute policies and programs to provide equal employment opportunities.
Sidney Frank Importing released a statement saying it denied the allegations and would move to dismiss the suit.

Debra Lynn Posen, Sidney Frank senior executive vice president, said in the statement that the two companies have a comprehensive sexual harassment policy and a set of guidelines to protect all employees including part-time promotional models.

The suit alleges that Sidney Frank, chairman of the importer, harassed the women with unwanted sexual touching that included grabbing their breasts and buttocks. The EEOC alleged that the acts were not isolated events, but part of regular working conditions since at least July 1993.
According to the suit most of the women worked as promotional models called "Jagerettes" who were required to attend dinner parties and other functions attended by Frank.
The suit alleged that, at these functions, Frank would attempt to "hug, tongue kiss and fondle the Jagerettes' breasts and buttocks."
It further alleges Frank offered clothing, trips and job opportunities to persuade Jagerettes to accept his sexual advances.
The suit also alleges that the women were harassed by other management and supervisory employees and their agents who engaged in similar unwanted touching and requests for sexual favors.
Women who complained were allegedly given less work or fired.
The EEOC alleged the models were also subjected to verbal and physical abuse when they were sent to promotional events at bars and other locations to encourage the sale of Jagermeister.
The companies also allegedly required employees to sign an arbitration agreement in which they agreed to give up their right to a jury trial and to seek compensatory and punitive damages.
The EEOC is also seeking a court ruling invalidating these agreements.
